# Statistical significance {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#statistical-significance"}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="80%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
> A result is statistically significant if, assuming the null hypothesis is true and the model assumptions hold, the probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as those observed (the p-value) is less than or equal to the chosen significance level α. This leads to rejection of the null hypothesis while controlling the long-run Type I error rate at α. (ChatGPT, 2026)
:::
:::

::: {.column width="20%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
![](images/week1/reaction.jpg){.absolute top=0 right=0 width="15%"}
:::
:::

:::

- [If this confuses you, you're not alone. It is deeply unintuitive.]{.fragment fragment-index=2}
- [We are going to scrap all of this conceptual baggage and start over.]{.fragment}



# You already understand probability {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#probability"}

_"Will it rain tomorrow?"_ [_"Probably not."_]{.fragment}

::: {.fragment}
That word, _probably_, is a probability. It's a way of talking about uncertainty, and
you use it every day.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- I don't know if it's going to rain tomorrow...
- ...but that doesn't mean I don't know anything.
- In Nepal, rain works differently in June than in January.
:::

::: {.fragment}
But what does _"a 31% chance of rain"_ actually mean? 
:::

::: {.incremental}
- Tomorrow's weather isn't a lottery. Specific physical factors decide it.
- The day isn't random [...but _**we**_ are uncertain about it.]{.blue} 
- 31% describes how certain we are about an uncertain fact.
:::

## Probability is just counting {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#counting"}

_Count everything that could happen. Count the ones you care about. Compare._

::: {.fragment}
- **Probability of rolling a six on a die**:\
  6 sides could land face up. Only one of them is a six.\
  [→ **1 out of 6**]{.blue}
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **Probability of winning a raffle**:\
  500 tickets sold. You bought 10.\
  [→ **10 out of 500**]{.blue}
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **The probability that a random person in this class came by bus**:\
  25 of you are here. 15 of you came by bus.\
  [→ **15 out of 25**]{.blue}.
:::

::: {.fragment}
You already knew how to do all three. Every analysis in this course comes down to
counting, exactly like this.
:::

## Counting the ways a thing could happen {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#counting-ways"}

_Flip a coin four times. How likely is exactly two heads?_

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r garden-all, opts.label = "garden"}
garden_plot(n = 4)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
```{r garden, opts.label = "garden"}
garden_plot(n = 4, target = 2)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.fragment}
Four events, two possibilities each:

- 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = **16** ways in all
- Exactly two heads: [**6** out of 16]{.blue}
:::

::: {.fragment}

| Heads | 0 | 1 | [2]{.blue} | 3 | 4 |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| **Ways** | 1 | 4 | [**6**]{.blue} | 4 | 1 |
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
What we're doing is simple:\
[We list all the ways the world could be, and count them.]{.blue}
:::

## Writing it down: 0 to 1 {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#convention-1"}

_New notation, not new ideas: a number from 0 to 1, or a percentage._

::: {.fragment}
| Number | Percentage | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0% | Something impossible |
| 0.02 | 2% | Winning the raffle: 10 ÷ 500 |
| 0.17 | 17% | Rolling a six: 1 ÷ 6 |
| 0.31 | 31% | Rain in Kathmandu: 113 ÷ 365 days[^rain-1] |
| 0.5 | 50% | A fair coin landing heads: 1 ÷ 2 |
| 1 | 100% | Something certain |

[^rain-1]: Kathmandu Airport weather station (NP000444540), NOAA GHCN-Daily, 2021–2025. A rainy day has at least 1 mm of rain. Days missing from the record are filled in at that month's average rate.
:::


::: {.fragment}
To convert between the two, move the decimal point two places right or left.
:::


## Writing it down: P(event) {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#convention-2"}

_We write the probability of an event as_ P( event ).

::: {.fragment}
| We write | We say | Value |
|---|---|---|
| P( rain tomorrow ) | "the probability of rain tomorrow" | 113 ÷ 365 ≈ 0.31 |
| P( getting heads ) | "the probability of getting heads" | 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5 |
| P( rolling a six ) | "the probability of rolling a six" | 1 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.17 |
| P( winning the raffle ) | "the probability of winning the raffle" | 10 ÷ 500 = 0.02 |
:::

::: {.fragment}
It's just shorthand. Everything inside the brackets is the thing we're unsure about.
:::

## Writing it down: P(event | condition) {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#rain"}

_We make a probability more specific by adding a condition._

- P( rain | July ) means [_"the probability of rain, given that it's July."_]{.blue}
  You already think this way: you carry an umbrella in July, not in December.

::: {.fragment}
|  | Rainy days[^rain-3] | Days counted | Probability | % |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| P( rain ) | 565 | 1,825 | **0.31** | (31%) |
| P( rain \| Apr ) | 35 | 150 | **0.23** | (23%) |
| P( rain \| Dec ) | 5 | 155 | **0.03** | (3%) |
| P( rain \| Jul ) | 126 | 155 | **0.81** | (81%) |
| P( rain \| Feb ) | 8 | 140 | **0.06** | (6%) |

[^rain-3]: Kathmandu Airport weather station (NP000444540), NOAA GHCN-Daily, 2021–2025. A rainy day has at least 1 mm of rain. Days missing from the record are filled in at that month's average rate.
:::



::: {.fragment}
Can data from the past five years help predict tomorrow? [Maybe, maybe not.]{.blue .fragment}
:::

## Probability lets us ask questions {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#lets-count"}

_Hands up if you had tea this morning._

{{< include _includes/week1/count-demo.md >}}

::: {.incremental}
- That's not really a probability yet. It's just a fact about this group.
- It becomes a **probability** when we use it to say something we _don't_ know:
  - _"If we pick one student at random, how likely is it they had tea?"_\
  [(You just worked it out: []{.count-k-out} in []{.count-n-out})]{.blue}
  - _"If we poll a random person on the street, how likely is it that they had tea?"_\
  [(Possibly similar, if we're willing to make a few assumptions.)]{.blue}
:::

::: {.fragment}
Every prediction needs assumptions. [Interesting predictions need strong assumptions.]{.blue}
:::

# Probability for Decision Making {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#applied-probability"}

::: {.fragment}
In Nepal, HIV has a prevalence of about 0.1%. We can write that as:
:::

::: {.incremental}
- P( HIV+ ) = 0.001 (0.1%)
:::

::: {.fragment}
With statistical tests and predictions, we talk about two kinds of accuracy:
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Sensitivity**: of the people who **have** HIV, the share who test positive.
  - P( test+ | HIV+ ) = **0.99** (true positive)
- **Specificity**: of the people who **don't have** HIV, the share who test negative.
  - P( test– | HIV– ) = **0.97** (true negative)
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Historical figures for older screening tests. Modern tests reach about 99.8% specificity, which still gives P( HIV+ | test+ ) of only about 33%. In practice, a positive screen is always confirmed with further tests, and the people who get tested aren't randomly selected.]{.source}
:::

## Prediction for Decision Making {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#base-rate"}

- Sensitivity P( test+ | HIV+ ): 99%
- Specificity P( test– | HIV– ): 97%

::: {.fragment fragment-index=0}
But there's something strange here...[it assumes the thing we want to know.]{.fragment fragment-index=1 .blue}
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
What we really want is P( HIV+ | test+): [3.2%]{.fragment fragment-index=3 .red}
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=4}

|[(pop: 100,000)]{.fragment fragment-index=5 .blue}           | Test+                                                            | Test–                                                             |
|----------|------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **HIV+**<br>[(0.1%&nbsp;=&nbsp;100)]{.fragment fragment-index=6 .blue}| P( Test+ \| HIV+ ): **99%**<br>_Sensitivity (True Positive)_<br>[(99)]{.fragment fragment-index=7 .blue}| P( Test– \| HIV+ ): **1%**<br>_Type II Error (False Negative)_<br>[(1)]{.fragment fragment-index=7 .blue}|
| **HIV–**<br>[(99.9%&nbsp;=&nbsp;99,900)]{.fragment fragment-index=6 .blue} | P( Test+ \| HIV– ): **3%**<br>_Type I Error (False Positive)_<br>[(2,997)]{.fragment fragment-index=7 .blue}| P( Test– \| HIV– ): **97%**<br>_Specificity (True Negative)_<br>[(96,903)]{.fragment fragment-index=7 .blue}|
:::

## Direction of conditions {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#direction"}

_Your intuitions about probability are good. They slip in one place: which way the
condition runs._ P(A|B) is not the same as P(B|A).

{{< include _includes/week1/cond-table.md >}}


# The base rate paradox {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#base-rate-paradox"}

_When something is rare, most positive results are false, even from an "accurate" test._

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {.r-stack}
::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r hiv-all, opts.label = "base_rate"}
base_rate_plot(n_true = 1, true_positives = 1, false_positives = 30)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
```{r hiv-tested, opts.label = "base_rate"}
base_rate_plot(
  n_true = 1,
  true_positives = 1,
  false_positives = 30,
  results = TRUE
)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
1,000 people get tested at random. Only [1 person has HIV]{.blue}. The test identifies them. 

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
It also flags [30 people who don't have HIV]{.red}.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
::: {.big-statement}
31 positives.\
Only 1 is real.
:::
:::
:::
:::

# Statistical significance (revisited) {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#statistical-significance-revisited"}

Let's look at that quote again:

> A result is statistically significant if, [assuming the null hypothesis is true]{.fragment fragment-index=2 .highlight-red} and the model assumptions hold, [the probability of obtaining data at least as extreme as those observed]{.fragment fragment-index=3 .highlight-blue} (the p-value) is less than or equal to the chosen significance level α. This leads to rejection of the null hypothesis while controlling the long-run Type I error rate at α.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
Two key phrases: 
:::

- ["assuming the null hypothesis is true"]{.fragment .red fragment-index=2}
- ["the probability of...data..."]{.fragment .blue fragment-index=3}

::: {.fragment}
How this frames statistical significance: P( [data]{.blue} | [hypothesis]{.red} )
:::

::: {.fragment}
How we intuitively think about data: P( [hypothesis]{.red} | [data]{.blue} )
:::


## The problem with p-values {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#pvalue-direction"}

If statistics has ever made you feel dumb or intimidated, [it's not you]{.blue}. Significance testing imagines the world [backwards]{.red} from our intuitions.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}

|  | Starts from | Asks |
|---|---|---|
| [**How&nbsp;we&nbsp;observe**]{.fragment fragment-index=2} | [what we [saw]{.blue}]{.fragment fragment-index=2} | [_"What does this tell me about the [world]{.green}?"_]{.fragment fragment-index=2} |
| [**A&nbsp;significance&nbsp;test**]{.fragment fragment-index=3} | [an [imagined world]{.red} with nothing going on]{.fragment fragment-index=3} | [_"How surprising would my [data]{.blue} be there?"_]{.fragment fragment-index=3} |
:::

::: {.incremental}
- A p-value doesn't tell you if a hypothesis is true.
- It tells you how unlikely this data would be if the null hypothesis were true.
- Those aren't the same thing. P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A)
:::

::: {.fragment}
Statistical significance works the opposite way that our intuitions do.
:::


# Bayesian Updating

## Bayesian Updating: What it is not
![*Statistical Rethinking*, p.2 (Richard McElreath, 2020)](images/week1/mcelreath-2.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

## Bayesian Updating: What it is {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#bayesian-updating"}

Instead of a flowchart of tests, updating is [**one rule for all of statistics**]{.blue}:

[**Prior**]{.red} × [**Likelihood**]{.blue} → [**Posterior**]{.green}

::: {.incremental}
- [**Prior**]{.red}: what we believed _before_ the new data
- [**Likelihood**]{.blue}: for _each_ possible answer, how expected were the data we saw?
- [**Posterior**]{.green}: what we believe _now_, with the new data taken into account
:::

::: {.fragment .callout-tip title="Example: will the mayor win?"}
::: {.incremental}
- [**Prior**]{.red}: _"He got 60% last time, so I think about 60% of Kathmandu will vote
  for him."_
- [**Likelihood**]{.blue}: _"Only 20% of my small survey said they'll vote for him. That would be surprising if his true support were 60%, but quite likely if it were around 20–30%."_
- [**Posterior**]{.green}: _"I now think about 45% of people will vote for him."_
:::
::: {.fragment }
Our posterior then becomes our prior for future observations.
:::
:::


## Bayesian Updating Example {.no-title}
```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
{{< include shiny/updating.R >}}
```


## Bayes' theorem {.mechanics notes="notes/week1_notes.md#bayes-theorem"}

_All of statistics in one formula._

{{< include _includes/week1/bayes-steps.md >}}

- [[**P( belief )**]{.red}: the **prior**. What we believed before.]{.fragment fragment-index=2}
- [[**P( data | belief )**]{.blue}: the **likelihood**. How likely the data are, if the belief is true.]{.fragment fragment-index=3}
- [[**P( belief | data )**]{.green}: the **posterior**. What we believe now.]{.fragment fragment-index=4}
- [[**P( data )**]{.gray}: Needed to rescale total possibilities to 100%. (Usually not interesting)]{.fragment fragment-index=5}

::: {.fragment fragment-index=6}
Conceptually:
[**Prior**]{.red} × [**Likelihood**]{.blue} → [**Posterior**]{.green}
:::

:::

58 discoveries.\
Only 8 are real.

:::
:::

## How far can we trust data? {.mechanics .smaller notes="notes/week1_notes.md#research-math"}

_**Sensitivity**, or **power**: if the idea is true, what is the chance of getting a significant result._\
_**Specificity**, or 1 − the **significance level** α: if the idea is false, what is the chance of not getting a significant result._

| Type of study | Base Rate | Sensitivity | Specificity | Chance a discovery is true |
|--------------------------------|:--------:|:-----:|:-----:|:------------:|
| Large trial of a treatment with strong earlier evidence | 50% | 80% | 95% | 94% |
| Small trial of a treatment with strong earlier evidence | 50% | 20% | 95% | 80% |
| Large study of a plausible new idea | 10% | 80% | 95% | 64% |
| Small study of a plausible new idea | 10% | 20% | 95% | [31%]{.red} |
| Large search for surprising new effects | 1% | 80% | 95% | [14%]{.red} |
| Small search for surprising new effects | 1% | 20% | 95% | [4%]{.red} |
| Small search, re-analysed until something is significant (p-hacked) | 1% | 20% | 80% | [1%]{.red} |



# Most studies are wrong... {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#is-that-a-problem"}

[...and that's okay.]{.fragment .blue}

::: {.incremental}
- A single study was never supposed to be the answer. It's just one observation.
- Each observation joins what we already know and nudges it, a little or a lot.
- We use observation to support or challenge what we think we already know.
- Without these prior assumptions, data are meaningless. Interesting claims need strong assumptions.
:::

## Hard data? {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#objective-subjective"}

> _"Qualitative research is subjective. Statistics is objective."_

::: {.fragment}
|                 | Observation                    | Interpretation assumes…                          |
|-----------------|--------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| **Qualitative** | interviews, field notes        | what people meant; where we chose to look; whose voices stand for others |
| **Quantitative**  | surveys, records, measurements | that the pattern isn't just chance; what causes what; how the data were generated |
:::

::: {.incremental}
- Observation gathers objective facts, but the way we gather those facts and interpret them is directly tied to assumptions.
- In both qualitative and quantitative work, we need strong assumptions to make interesting claims.
:::

## Science is updating {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#science-is-updating"}

What makes science work isn't experiments or observations.

::: {.fragment}
It's [groups of scientists arguing]{.blue} about how to fit many (often contradictory)
experiments and observations together.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- [**Assume**]{.red}: a prior, written down where others can argue with it.
- [**Look**]{.blue}: new data test it.
- [**Update**]{.green}: the posterior, which is the starting point next time.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.big-statement}
Science isn't the experiments we do.\
It's the debates we have about them.
:::
:::

## Is noise the only problem? {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#best-case"}

Everything today has been about [noise]{.blue}: chance results, small samples, false
positives. Noise is the problem [more data can fix]{.blue}.

::: {.fragment}
But a pattern can be real, show up again in every new dataset, and still not mean what
it seems.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.big-statement}
Next week: the other way data mislead.
:::
:::

# Doing science {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#doing-science"}

_The math is the least interesting part of statistics._

::: {.incremental}
- Nearly every important choice happens before any numbers: what to ask, what to
  observe, who to include, what to assume.
- After we've gathered our data, they never speak for themselves. We interpret them in
  terms of what we already know.
- So we can interpret and critique a statistical argument without the statistical
  mechanics.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.big-statement}
The science comes first.
:::
:::

# What's ahead {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#whats-ahead"}

| Week | Topic | Punchline |
|:-:|---|---|
| **1** | Updating | Data are noisy. Science is updating. |
| **2** | Distributions | [Think in distributions.]{.line} [A pattern can mislead by chance, or by a hidden cause.]{.line} |
| **3** | Models | [Draw your assumptions.]{.line} [What you include can flip the answer.]{.line} |
| **4** | Confounders | What to control for depends on the causal story, not the data. |
| **5** | Evaluating&nbsp;research | Ask what's in the world that isn't in their model. |

# Practical work: Will the mayor win? {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-demo"}

_Appendix: we'll work through this together with the TA in our second class._

Let's walk through the simplest possible version of the full Bayesian workflow (next slide).

- **Estimand**: θ, the share of Kathmandu voters who will vote for the current mayor.
- **Background**: in the last election, the mayor got 60% of the vote.
- **Data**: we survey *n* voters at random, and *k* of them say they will vote for the mayor.

::: {.callout-note title="A deliberately simple model"}
Each respondent is like a coin flip that comes up "mayor" with probability θ. No weighting,
no turnout, no non-response, no post-stratification. We'll add those later.
:::

## The Bayesian workflow {.smaller .mechanics}

{{< include _includes/bayesian-workflow.md >}}

## The model, written formally {.mechanics notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-model"}

$$
\begin{aligned}
k &\sim \text{Binomial}(n,\ \theta) && \class{blue}{\text{likelihood}} \\
\theta &\sim \text{your prior} && \class{red}{\text{prior}}
\end{aligned}
$$

| Symbol | Read it as | In our survey |
|---|---|---|
| $n$ | the number of people surveyed | 20: data, we know it |
| $k$ | how many of them said "mayor" | 4: data, we know it |
| $\theta$ | the mayor's share among all voters | unknown: what we want to learn |
| $\sim$ | "is drawn from" | |

::: {.incremental}
- [**Line 1**]{.blue}: each person we ask is a coin flip that lands "mayor" with chance θ.
- [**Line 2**]{.red}: what we believe about θ before asking anyone.
- From Week 3 on, we'll build models like this visually.
:::

## Step 1: The prior {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-prior"}

_Before seeing any survey, what do you believe about θ? Drag the points._

{{< include _includes/week1/poll-prior.md >}}

## Step 2: The likelihood {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-likelihood"}

_Set the survey. How likely is that result, for each possible value of θ?_

{{< include _includes/week1/poll-likelihood.md >}}

The likelihood is **not** a belief. It's what our model of the survey (each answer like a coin flip) says about our data, one candidate value of θ at a time.

## Step 3: Prior × likelihood → posterior {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-posterior"}

{{< include _includes/week1/poll-posterior.md >}}

## Survey 1, by hand {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-by-hand"}

```{r poll-demo, include=FALSE}
steps <- poll_sequence()
s1 <- POLL_SURVEYS[[1]]
s2 <- POLL_SURVEYS[[2]]
s3 <- POLL_BIG_SURVEY
hand <- poll_by_hand()
```

_A worked example with one fixed prior: about `r pct(round(steps$guess[1], 1))`, as in the last
election. Then survey 1: `r s1[["k"]]` of `r s1[["n"]]` say "mayor"._

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{r poll-update, opts.label = "half"}
poll_update_plot()
```
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
| θ | `r hand$theta[1]` | `r hand$theta[2]` | `r hand$theta[3]` |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| [**Prior**]{.red} (height) | `r hand$prior[1]` | `r hand$prior[2]` | `r hand$prior[3]` |
| [**Likelihood**]{.blue} | `r hand$likelihood[1]` | `r hand$likelihood[2]` | `r hand$likelihood[3]` |
| Prior × likelihood | `r hand$product[1]` | [**`r hand$product[2]`**]{.green} | `r hand$product[3]` |

::: {.fragment}
Do this at every θ, then rescale so the total is 100%. That's the
[**posterior**]{.green}.
:::

::: {.fragment}
It lands where both find θ plausible: not `r hand$theta[1]` (the prior rules it
out), not `r hand$theta[3]` (the data do).
:::
:::
:::

## Today's posterior is tomorrow's prior {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-sequence"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{r poll-sequence, opts.label = "half"}
poll_sequence_plot(steps)
```

Survey 1: `r s1[["k"]]` of `r s1[["n"]]` said "mayor". Survey 2: `r s2[["k"]]` of `r s2[["n"]]`.
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
| | Best&nbsp;guess | 90%&nbsp;range |
|---|--:|--:|
| [**Prior**]{.red} | `r pct(steps$guess[1])` | `r steps$range[1]` |
| After&nbsp;survey&nbsp;1 | `r pct(steps$guess[2])` | `r steps$range[2]` |
| After&nbsp;survey&nbsp;2 | [**`r pct(steps$guess[3])`**]{.green} | `r steps$range[3]` |

::: {.fragment}
Each row is Bayes' theorem:\
$\class{green}{P(\theta \mid \text{survey})} \propto \class{blue}{P(\text{survey} \mid \theta)} \times \class{red}{P(\theta)}$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Survey 1's posterior is survey 2's prior. Updating once on all
`r s1[["n"]] + s2[["n"]]` people (`r s1[["k"]] + s2[["k"]]` of `r s1[["n"]] + s2[["n"]]`) gives the same answer.
:::
:::
:::

## Different priors, same data {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-converge"}

```{r poll-converge-numbers, include=FALSE}
beliefs <- poll_converge()
supporter <- beliefs$guess[beliefs$who == "Supporter"]
skeptic <- beliefs$guess[beliefs$who == "Skeptic"]
gap <- round(100 * supporter) - round(100 * skeptic) # as the table shows them
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{r poll-converge, opts.label = "half_tall"}
poll_converge_plot(beliefs)
```
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
| Best guess | [**Supporter**]{.orange} | **Skeptic** |
|---|--:|--:|
| `r levels(beliefs$stage)[1]` | `r pct(supporter[1])` | `r pct(skeptic[1])` |
| `r levels(beliefs$stage)[2]` | `r pct(supporter[2])` | `r pct(skeptic[2])` |
| `r levels(beliefs$stage)[3]` | `r pct(supporter[3])` | `r pct(skeptic[3])` |

Survey 3 is a bigger poll: `r s3[["k"]]` of `r s3[["n"]]` say "mayor".

::: {.fragment}
They start `r gap[1]` points apart and end `r gap[3]` apart. A prior is where you start,
not where you end up.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Except for certainty: if you rule a value out (a prior of 0), no data can bring it back.
:::
:::
:::

## Answering the question {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-answer"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{r poll-majority, opts.label = "half"}
poll_majority_plot(steps)
```
:::

::: {.column width="54%"}
_Will he get more than half the vote?_ Add up the belief above 50%.

| | P( more than half ) |
|---|--:|
| [**Prior**]{.red} | `r pct(steps$majority[1])` |
| After survey 1 | `r pct(steps$majority[2])` |
| After survey 2 | [**`r pct(steps$majority[3])`**]{.green} |

::: {.fragment}
That's P( [hypothesis]{.red} | [data]{.blue} ): the question a p-value can't answer.
:::

::: {.fragment}
And it says how sure we are: not "he'll lose", but about a 1 in
`r round(1 / steps$majority[3])` chance of a majority.
:::
:::
:::

## What to try {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#poll-try"}

- **Flat prior vs. strong prior.** Draw a flat prior, then a narrow one around 60% (last
  election). With the same survey, how far apart are the posteriors?
- **More data.** On Step 2, keep the survey at 20% but raise *n* from 20 to 500. What happens
  to the prior's influence?
- **Updating in sequence.** Make the posterior your new prior, then set a second survey on
  Step 2. Yesterday's posterior is today's prior.
- **Answering the real question.** P( mayor wins ) is a direct statement about the hypothesis
  given the data: [P( hypothesis | data )]{.green}, not a p-value.

*What is the result, and how much does it depend on our assumptions?* This is that question,
in miniature.


# More resources {notes="notes/week1_notes.md#more-resources"}

This course draws heavily on the work of Richard McElreath, a statistician working out of the Max Planck Institute. If you want a deeper dive into statistical mechanics, consider the resources below.

- **The book:** Richard McElreath,
  [*Statistical Rethinking: A Bayesian Course with Examples in R and Stan*](https://xcelab.net/rm/)
  (2nd edition, 2020). This course follows its approach.
- **The lectures:** McElreath's
  [Statistical Rethinking 2026](https://github.com/rmcelreath/stat_rethinking_2026)
  series on YouTube. Twenty free lectures that follow the book.
